newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Strong UK trade data calm strong pound fears.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Strong UK trade data calm strong pound fears.

text.p: Britain's trade deficit with the rest of the world narrowed in January, according to official data on Wednesday, suggesting fears that the pound's strength has hurt exporters are premature.

The Office of National Statistics (ONS) said the global trade deficit appeared to be narrowing with exports rising slightly and imports flat. January's trade gap was 641 million pounds ($1 billion), down from 825 million the previous month.
Analysts also welcomed the figures, which were slightly better than forecast, saying they showed the effect of the strong pound and high domestic demand had yet to surface.

"The figures are a bit better than expected. Exports are showing decent gains in nominal terms," said Bank of America analyst Jeremy Hawkins. "Some of the worries over the rise of the pound and the loss of competitiveness may be overdone."

The pound has rallied steadily over the last eight months, and, despite a recent flutter this month after the British election date was set, is up nearly 17 percent on a trade-weighted basis from last August.
The trend has fuelled fears the high exchange rate will depress exports by pushing prices up for overseas buyers.
Analysts said while Wednesday's figures eased worries for the short-term, they expected the trade deficit to increase later in the year as the loss of competitiveness took its toll.

"It's later in the year that we're going to see the full effect of sterling and strong domestic demand in these numbers," said James Barty, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "At the moment you've got the lagged effect of sterling being quite weak in the middle of last year...we would expect the figures to deteriorate in the second half of the year."
Economists expect the impact to be delayed because export volumes react more slowly to higher prices than import costs which show an immediate cut and hence improve trade figures in value terms.

The data, which also showed the non-EU trade deficit for February grew slightly less than expected, gave a brief fillip to the pound and UK government bonds. The non-EU trade deficit was 554 million pounds, compared to 339 million in January.
The figures reinforce Monday's data showing the UK's current account almost in balance and follow a stream of UK data highlighting the robustness of Britain's economy.

The ruling Conservative Party has been trumpeting the health of the economy in a bid to boost its ailing poll ratings ahead of the May 1 election. It is currently more than 20 points behind the opposition Labour party.
